network.title: Service boundary map
network.objective: Map the scoped services and compare a closed-port control.
network.prompt: Map the scoped fixture, compare open and closed ports, verify HTTP and TLS, and report only observed service behavior.
network.summary: The investigation checks a negative port control before correlating DNS, services, HTTP, and certificate evidence.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: I will query the lab DNS server directly. The result will establish the local address before service discovery.
DNS is confirmed. I will map only the three scoped service ports; an open port alone will not establish a vulnerability.
The ports are reachable. I will verify service behavior with version detection and retain both text and XML output.
I will confirm that the discovered HTTP service responds, retaining the response as a file.
The HTTP service is healthy. I will inspect its declared routes before interpreting what the application exposes.
I will verify the lab certificate with its supplied CA; I will not disable certificate validation.
I will inspect the structured scan artifact before writing the inventory. The report should distinguish discovery from verified application behavior.
The negative-control port should not look like an exposed service. I will save its actual result before drawing a network boundary.
I will include the negative control in the report so coverage is explicit.

services.prompt: Compare the local service identity and build with a supplied synthetic advisory and SearchSploit leads. Reject a product mismatch and report remaining uncertainty.
services.summary: A broad exploit hit is read, then rejected against the fixture's observed product and local advisory. No CVE is invented for the synthetic app.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: DNS is confirmed. I will map only the three scoped service ports; an open port alone will not establish a vulnerability.
I will obtain service-detection evidence before consulting vulnerability references.

I will verify the administrative route's actual response. A 403 is an access-control observation, not evidence of compromise.

website.title: Web and API exposure
website.objective: Verify a web exposure and reject unauthenticated API guesses.
website.prompt: Discover the local application's routes, compare unauthenticated API and debug behavior, reject a missing backup route, and verify one exposure independently.
website.summary: A bounded fuzz, a local Nuclei matcher, HTTP controls, and browser confirmation establish the debug exposure while the profile API and backup guesses are rejected.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: I will discover only the fixture's small route list, with bounded concurrency and a retained tool result.
Directory discovery found a lead. I will fingerprint the actual application before selecting a verification check.

arguments.content:
id: hercules-lab-debug
info:
  name: Disposable Atlas debug endpoint
  author: hercules-showcase
  severity: info
http:
  - method: GET
    path:
      - '{{BaseURL}}/debug'
    matchers-condition: and
    matchers:
      - type: status
        status: [200]
      - type: word
        words: ['"debug": true', 'disposable']
        condition: and

operations.observation: I will author a local Nuclei check requiring both HTTP 200 and the explicit disposable debug marker.
I will run only this local template. Built-in online template updates and interactsh are disabled.
I will test the suspected backup route independently. Its normal 404 must be rejected rather than counted as an exposure.
Before browser operations, I will read Hercules's actual browser guidance and use fresh snapshots for targeting.
I will confirm the debug response in the browser before accepting the scanner lead.
The browser confirms the disposable debug data. I will document this limited exposure without inventing credentials or exploitability.
I will save visual evidence alongside the raw HTTP and scanner artifacts.
The profile endpoint is a separate hypothesis. I will test it without a session rather than assume the debug exposure grants account access.
The API rejects unauthenticated access. I will keep this negative control out of the findings list.

forensics.title: Binary and layered forensics
forensics.objective: Triage a binary, follow file clues, and reject a decoy.
forensics.prompt: Triage a supplied ELF header, then follow PCAP, image, archive and encryption clues. Reject the wrong key and decoy before accepting a checksum-verified result.
forensics.summary: Binutils establish the binary's limits; packet fragments lead to an appended archive, a failed decryption hypothesis, and a digest-checked result.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: I will identify the supplied binary and inspect its header and strings before inferring what it does. It has no executable program to decompile.
I will establish file types and hashes before modifying or extracting any challenge input.

arguments.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json,struct
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('/opt/workspace/challenge/route.pcap').read_bytes(); cursor=24; clues=[]
while cursor<len(p):
    ts,us,size,orig=struct.unpack_from('<IIII',p,cursor); cursor+=16
    packet=p[cursor:cursor+size]; cursor+=size
    clue=json.loads(packet[42:]); clues.append(clue)
assert [c['sequence'] for c in clues]==[1,2,3]
print(json.dumps({'packets':clues,'next':'Inspect the carrier, then apply the route rule from its archive manifest.'},indent=2))
PY

operations.observation: I will inspect the real packet payloads in sequence and retain their route fragments as clues, without assuming they are the final answer.
The packets name the carrier. I will check its embedded signatures before choosing an extraction method.
The carrier contains a clue about multiple endings. I will inspect the archive as a separate layer, rather than treat the image's first signature as complete.

arguments.command:
mkdir -p /opt/workspace/artifacts/forensics; python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
from zipfile import ZipFile
p=Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/forensics')
with ZipFile('/opt/workspace/challenge/carrier.png') as z:
 print(z.namelist()); z.extractall(p)
PY

operations.observation: The appended ZIP is confirmed. I will extract the locally authored entries into a separate evidence directory and inspect the manifest.
The manifest specifies AES-256-CBC, PBKDF2 and zlib, and says to join packet fragments with hyphens. I will test the key construction against those clues.
I will reject the tempting unseparated-route hypothesis. A failed decryption is evidence to revise the key construction.
The manifest's separators matter. I will derive the key from the observed packet sequence and decrypt the actual payload.

arguments.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import hashlib,json,zlib
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/forensics'); m=json.loads((p/'manifest.json').read_text())
flag=zlib.decompress((p/'decrypted.bin').read_bytes()); digest=hashlib.sha256(flag).hexdigest()
decoy=(p/'decoy.txt').read_bytes().strip(); decoy_digest=hashlib.sha256(decoy).hexdigest()
assert digest==m['flag_sha256'] and decoy_digest!=digest
result={'flag':flag.decode(),'sha256':digest,'checksum_match':True,'decoy_match':False}
(p/'verification.json').write_text(json.dumps(result,indent=2)); print(json.dumps(result,indent=2))
PY

operations.observation: I will apply the discovered compression layer, compare the recovered flag's SHA-256 with the manifest, and reject the decoy by its mismatching digest.
The checksum and decoy checks passed. I will reread the verification artifact before publishing the reproducible write-up.

web-ctf.title: Chained web CTF
web-ctf.objective: Combine browser state and an API header, then verify the result.
web-ctf.prompt: Follow local route clues through browser state and an API header. Reject a plausible decoy and a request missing one prerequisite, then verify the actual result by digest.
web-ctf.summary: A route needs both session state and a header. A cookie-only request and an inconsistent decoy are rejected before the final digest passes.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: I will inspect declared routes before guessing endpoints.
The draft API is listed. I will test its unauthenticated behavior before exploring browser state.
I will preserve the rejected request. It should tell us which prerequisite is missing.
Before browser operations, I will read Hercules's actual browser guidance and use fresh snapshots for targeting.
The challenge offers a draft-session bootstrap. I will follow that local clue in the actual browser.
The page reveals a route-header requirement. I will combine it with the disposable session cookie instead of putting the value in the URL.
The cookie alone may be insufficient. I will retain that negative control before sending the discovered header.
The rejection names the missing prerequisite; I will not count this branch as a solved challenge.
A separate candidate is available. I will check its digest before accepting the first flag-like string.

arguments.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import hashlib,json
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/decoy.json'); d=json.loads(p.read_text()[p.read_text().index('{'):]); assert hashlib.sha256(d['flag'].encode()).hexdigest()!=d['sha256']; print('decoy checksum mismatch; rejected')

Both prerequisites are now observed. I will send the scoped request and save the actual response.

arguments.command:

from pathlib import Path
p=Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/draft-flag.txt'); raw=p.read_text(); data=json.loads(raw[raw.index('{'):]); digest=hashlib.sha256(data['flag'].encode()).hexdigest(); assert digest==data['sha256']; print(json.dumps({'flag':data['flag'],'checksum_match':True,'sha256':digest})); Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/web-ctf-verification.json').write_text(json.dumps(data,indent=2))

I will confirm that the discovered HTTP service responds, retaining the response as a file.
The review log is larger than a concise inline answer. I will read its first bounded page and note that these are supplied inputs, not current scanner results.

p=Path('/opt/workspace/review-log.ndjson'); records=[json.loads(s) for s in p.read_text().splitlines()]; summary={'records':len(records),'debug_records':sum(r['path']=='/debug' for r in records),'source':'authored lab input','fresh_evidence':'artifacts/health.txt'}; Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts/reconciled.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2)); print(json.dumps(summary,indent=2))

recovery.title: Timeout and job recovery

recovery.prompt: Run a bounded background probe, preserve timeout diagnostics, check the exact managed job ID, and narrow the request before concluding whether the service is available.
recovery.summary: The first request times out; a scoped health probe succeeds. The job inventory and partial output prevent a false outage claim.
phases: Establish scope and start the runtime
Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

arguments.command: mkdir -p /opt/workspace/artifacts; echo 'Starting scoped lab probe'; curl -sS --max-time 1 http://172.30.42.10:8000/slow > /opt/workspace/artifacts/slow-partial.txt 2>&1; echo 'Slow endpoint exceeded the bounded request timeout'; sleep 1; echo 'Narrow the next check to /health'

operations.observation: I will start a bounded background request and retain its output. A slow service should not stall the entire investigation.
I will inspect the job using the ID Hercules actually returned, keeping partial output visible.
I will inspect Hercules's current managed-job inventory; a harness task identifier would not identify this shell job.

I will confirm that the discovered HTTP service responds, retaining the response as a file.
The narrow health request succeeded. This confirms a slow endpoint rather than a complete service outage.
I will verify the background job's final state before cleanup and reporting.

recheck.title: Remediation proof
recheck.objective: Compare before and after evidence for a local remediation.
recheck.prompt: Capture a vulnerable local baseline, apply the disposable fixture change, repeat identical requests, and prove that the debug route closes while the application stays healthy.
recheck.summary: Independent before/after artifacts prove the debug route closes, security headers appear, and the health endpoint remains available.

Investigate and verify the evidence
Report and clean up the owned runtime

operations.observation: I will capture the baseline response before changing the disposable configuration.
The baseline confirms the fixture debug endpoint. I will retain it for a direct before/after comparison.
I will apply only the explicitly scoped fixture remediation. This changes no production or external service.
I will repeat the same debug request after the change, keeping its response separate from the baseline.
The endpoint now returns 404. I will verify the new headers and compare the two saved responses.
I will confirm that the application remains healthy after remediation.

arguments.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('/opt/workspace/artifacts'); before=(p/'before.txt').read_text(); after=(p/'after.txt').read_text(); assert '200 OK' in before and '404 Not Found' in after and 'Content-Security-Policy' in after and 'X-Content-Type-Options' in after; r={'baseline_debug':True,'debug_closed':True,'csp_present':True,'nosniff_present':True}; (p/'comparison.json').write_text(json.dumps(r,indent=2)); print(json.dumps(r,indent=2))
PY
